messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Moses came to the first session with his shoulders hunched forward, as though bracing against a wind only he could feel. At nineteen, he was the youngest detective in his precinct, a fact that had once filled him with pride. Now it felt like a target. Six months earlier, he had been taken. The details came out in fragments over several meetings, each word pulled from him like a splinter. He had responded to a routine call about a domestic disturbance in a basement apartment on the south side. When he entered, the door swung shut behind him and locked. Three men were waiting. They kept him for eleven hours, bound to a chair with zip ties, while they demanded information about an ongoing narcotics investigation. He gave them nothing, but they did not believe him. They took turns. The things he heard during those hours—the wet sound of a belt being pulled through its loops, the low hum of a space heater that clicked on and off, the way one of them whistled tunelessly between questions—those sounds had lodged themselves inside his skull. He could not find the words to describe what happened, even now. When he tried, his throat closed. He knew the sequence of events, could recite the facts in a deposition, but the shape of the experience itself remained formless, unspeakable. What came instead were the sounds. At night, lying next to his girlfriend, he would hear the belt again, or the click of the heater, and his body would go rigid. Sometimes the terror arrived without any image at all—just a wave of heat and dread that rose from nowhere, leaving him shaking and nauseous on the bathroom floor.

The world outside had become a threat. Moses stopped going out after dark. He told his girlfriend it was because he was tired from work, but the truth was simpler and more absolute: night was when they had taken him, and night felt like a room with a closing door. He worked double shifts to avoid the sunset, then came home and sat in the dark apartment with the television off, listening. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down—if he let himself feel safe—something would find him. Physical contact had become unbearable. When his girlfriend reached for his hand, he flinched. When a colleague clapped him on the shoulder, he felt a spike of adrenaline so sharp it left him dizzy. He had always been a tactile person; now he kept his arms crossed, his body angled away from everyone. She had started sleeping on the couch, not because he asked her to, but because she could not stand the way he stiffened when she rolled toward him in bed. He saw the hurt in her face and told himself he would fix it tomorrow. Tomorrow never came.

The suppression was a full-time job. He tried not to think about the basement. He tried not to think about the zip ties or the whistling or the way the space heater had smelled of burning dust. He pushed the memories down so hard that they migrated into his body instead. His jaw ached from clenching. His hands trembled during briefings. He became known at the precinct as the detective who never stayed for the debrief, who left the moment the lights came on in the parking lot. His captain had pulled him aside twice and asked if he was alright. Moses said he was fine. He had become an expert at saying he was fine.

What finally brought him in was the night he came home to find his girlfriend packing a bag. She was crying. She said she loved him but she could not live in a house where she was treated like a threat. He watched her leave and felt nothing at first—just the familiar numbness—and then, hours later, the wave hit him without any image at all. He was on the floor, gasping, and he had no idea why. The next morning he called the department's employee assistance line. He told the intake worker that he needed to talk to someone. He did not say what about. He still could not find the words. But he was afraid that if he kept going like this—alone in his apartment, jumping at every sound, pushing away the person who loved him—he would lose everything he had left. He was not sure he deserved to keep it. But he was here. That was the first thing.
